name: Mujadara: Lentils & Rice with Crispy Onions
why: A beloved Levantine one-pot classic that's vegan, gluten-free, and costs almost nothing — the whole dish is a 40-minute low-and-slow onion caramelisation lesson that transforms humble lentils and rice into something deeply caramel-sweet and smoky. Perfect October comfort food, and the crispy fried onion rings on top make it look far fancier than it is.
author: Henry
ingredients: 1 cup black lentils, sorted and rinsed
1 cup long-grain white rice, soaked 10-15 min then drained
1 large yellow onion, cut into very thin rings (for frying)
1/4 cup extra virgin olive oil (plus 2-3 tbsp more for frying)
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

steps: Sort and rinse the black lentils under cold water.
Soak the rice in water for 10-15 minutes, then drain.
Dice 2 large yellow onions (about 4 cups) and cut 1 more into very thin rings.
Chop the parsley and set aside.
Par-boil the lentils: put them in a small saucepan over high heat with 2 cups of water. Bring to a boil, reduce to medium-low, cover, and simmer until just tender, 10-12 minutes. Drain and set aside.

Start the onions: in a large sauté pan with a lid, heat the 1/4 cup olive oil over medium-high heat. Add the diced onions and cook until they are dark golden brown — darker than your typical caramelised onions — about 40 minutes. Sprinkle with the 1 tsp salt as they cook and stir every few minutes so nothing burns.
Carefully add 2 cups of water to the onions (it will splatter), bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to low and simmer 2 minutes.
Stir in the soaked rice, par-cooked lentils, a good dash of kosher salt, black pepper, and the cumin.
Reduce heat to low, cover, and cook until the liquid is absorbed and the rice is tender, 15-20 minutes.

Meanwhile, fry the onion rings: in a large skillet over medium-high heat, add 2-3 tbsp olive oil. Test with a small piece of onion — when it bubbles vigorously, the oil is ready. Fry the rings in batches until crisp and deeply golden, about 1-2 minutes per batch. Drain on a paper-towel-lined plate.
Let the mujadara rest, covered, for 10 minutes undisturbed.
Transfer to serving bowls, top with the crispy onion rings, and garnish with parsley.

pro_tips: The onions must go darker than normal caramelised onions — keep them on medium-high and don't panic when they look nearly black at the edges; that's exactly what gives mujadara its deep sweetness.
The recipe is also traditionally made with bulgur instead of rice (Syrian style) — a 1:1 swap works great for a different texture. Serves with a simple salad of tomatoes, cucumber, and lemony tahini.
